correctness.rationale: The normalized disk and boundary norms give reciprocal squared norms a_n=(n+1)/(1+κ(n+1)) with one constant and two harmonic modes per positive n. Writing a_n as a constant minus a moment yields exactly the Poisson-mixture identity. Dividing by the positive P_r, differentiation under the s-integral gives strict angular increase in c=cos θ: the numerator of the c-derivative of P_sr/P_r is proportional to −r(1−s)(1−sr²)(1−s²r²). At c=1 the normalized kernel is positive. At c=−1 the ratio (1+r)(1−sr)/((1−r)(1+sr)) increases strictly with r for s<1, and the integral diverges as r→1. This gives the unique first crossing and exactly two zeros at every larger radius. Nonzero angular derivative away from the antipodal point and nonzero radial derivative at it give the embedded analytic arc. For each c<1 the Poisson term tends to zero and the integral to a positive number (dominated, as the denominator is bounded away from zero for fixed c), so the zero cosine tends to 1. The compact κ→0 limit on the negative axis crosses at √2−1. The κ-scaled kernel tends to P_r for fixed r as κ→∞, forcing ρ_κ→1; taking the limit in the exact root equation gives κ(1−ρ_κ)→2∫₀¹(1−s)/(1+s) ds. The attached checker and logged values are consistent finite numerical checks, not proof of any continuum assertion.
